utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have problems with the translation. The channel that I have is 4, and I am not getting English. (NO ENGLISH TRANSLATION)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We will have a break for five minutes to settle the matter. --- Recess at 9.12 a.m. --- Resumed at 9.20 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We can proceed now. I believe that everything has been straightened out. It has. Thank you. Mr. Niemann, can you hear the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So we can continue. We shall continue with the testimony of Professor Bianchini, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, can Professor Bianchini be brought in? Thank you. Stefano Bianchini (continued)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Professor Bianchini, how are you feeling? Are you feeling okay in this new courtroom? You can be seated. You have already taken the oath, and you will continue to answer the questions posed to you by Prosecutor Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, yesterday, just before the break, we had reached the stage where you had embarked upon a discussion of the conflict that was to emerge between the Bosnian Croats and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and you had proceeded to show us some maps which reflected the respective claims of the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats. Moving on in that vein, can you tell us who it was or what organisations represented the political and military interests of the Bosnian Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In an interview by Stjepan Klujic -- Stjepan Klujic was the President of HDZ in Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1990 up to February 1992 -- he proudly described himself as a man of Tudjman. Generally the relations between the HDZ in Bosnia and the HDZ in Croatia were known to be very closed. Very often the members of the presidency of the HDZ in Bosnia went to Zagreb to discuss common matters of interest. So this declaration, which is interesting, was given to a journalist of Bosnia, Goran Tordovic 0003 (phonetic) and published in a book, in a collection of articles. It is just to give you an idea of what the connection was between the leadership of Herceg-Bosna and Zagreb and how they proudly confirmed this, taking into account that even -- sometimes there not complete agreement between this leadership and Zagreb, particularly in the case of Stjepan Klujic who consistently defended the idea of saving the independence and integrity of Bosnia. For this reason, he was removed in February 1992. But there are other elements that can confirm this particular relation between Zagreb, and between the HDZ in Zagreb and the HDZ in Herceg-Bosna. The role of the Minister of Defence, Gojko Susak is crucial in this sense. Gojko Susak was a Herzegovinian. He was born in Herzegovina, and he was known, even in Croatia, as the most representative of the Herzegovina lobby in the government of Croatia. We have documents that show the kind of relations between Gojko Susak and HDZ. Very often 21 the HDZ in Herceg-Bosna sent letters or asked Gojko 22 Susak for help, for instance, even to receive a supply of weapons. A document, an interesting document, has been published. It was confidential, in fact. It was a document prepared last year by the OSCE. This document, albeit confidential, was published in Sarajevo by a monthly Dani. In this document, the OSCE officials give information, very wide information, about the role of Herceg-Bosna and Zagreb in their -- and their mutual relations. According to this document, for instance, Gojko Susak and Miroslav Tudjman, the son of the President of the Republic, crucially contributed in supplying, supporting, and sending weapons to HVO during the war through a private enterprise named Alan, A-L-A-N, which later became, according to this document, a state enterprise, R.H. Alan, and so in this document, this was particularly focused. It's also true that the opposition in the parliament -- in the Sabor, in the parliament in Zagreb, tried several times to know the percentage of the Croat budget sent to Herceg-Bosna for military and civilian help. But even in this case, HDZ in Zagreb regularly opposed giving this kind of information to the opposition. I have also a document which is interesting, and if the Court allows, I can give you some details and I can refresh my memory looking at the documents I have with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a document of June 1992. It has been -- the letterhead is "Republic of Croatia, Ministry of Defence, Zagreb," it is signed by Defence Minister Gojko Susak and is an order -- it's an order to send 13 persons to the southern front. The southern front was the front directed by Janko Bobetko, and these persons were on the southern front which was formally, which had to be considered formally, southern Dalmatia from Split to Dubrovnik, but as many documents confirm, this southern front included a large part of Herzegovina, even Mostar and sometimes Nevesinje. So this document is interesting. Why? Because it is followed by another document of March 1993. This means June, March, eight, nine months later. This document comes from the HVO and is signed by the deputy head of the army command of the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna, Miro Andric. In this document you can find a person, Mr. Zlatic, who is included in the letter of Gojko Susak eight months earlier, in which it is written that Mr. Zlatic fulfilled his tasks on the southern battlefield. This is a document of HVO sent from Mostar to the person -- to the Croatian army, the 101 air brigade, and it's written that he fulfilled his tasks and must reserve all pertaining rights, obligations. In this sense, they make free Zlatic to come back to the Croatian army from the HVO brigades. So this shows a kind of linkage from the Croatian army, sending in person to the southern front which is, in fact, something not related only on the territory of Croatia, and these persons were later made free by HVO in order to allow them to come back to Croatia. So this seems to me an interesting document that can confirm these kind of relations between the two parts and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, in your researches -- I think before we go on to that. Can you just basically give us a very brief description of what was the HDZ and what was the HVO and the HV, because these are terms which are used -- I think it should be clear what we are referring to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. HDZ is a political party and worked as a political party. It was created before the election of 1990. We had opportunity to speak about it -- about it, in the last session. HDZ is quite clear institution. About HVO. HVO was formally established on April 8, 1992, that is two days after the official eruption of the war. In fact, HVO already existed earlier. A group of -- as an instrument of defending Croat people. It was connected particularly -- it was organised particularly after the events in Ravno which took place in October 1991 when Ravno was burned by Serb irregulars backed by JNA. HVO was -- when the HVO was created in -- formally in October -- in, sorry, in April 1992, it was created as the armed organisation, the defence organisation, of the Croat people in Herceg-Bosna. This HVO, this organisation, was restructured in July, between July and August, in the following months, and in July it was transformed into a temporarily military government in a way, structured in different sections with local administrative organisation distributed in Herceg-Bosna. And until August 3rd, the President of HVO was Mate Boban who was also the President of Herceg-Bosna. And then after August 14, he made a decision to resign and other persons were appointed by him directly as the President and later Vice-Presidents of HVO. So this is an organisation with these kind of characteristics later, and what is important to stress is that anyway, the Presidents and the Vice-Presidents and the other members of the HVO were liable for their actions to the President of Herceg-Bosna. So in this case, Mate Boban maintained control, strict control, over HVO. HVO and HDZ. I don't remember if -- you asked me another organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the HV.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HV is the Croat army, Hrvatska was the Croat army. HV is the Croat army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what was the role played by Herceg-Bosna as an autonomous region?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Herceg-Bosna played a very interesting role in the sense that the authorities of Herceg-Bosna tried to establish full control over the area of Herceg-Bosna. I had the opportunity to read 300 pages of the official gazette of Herceg-Bosna published between the autumn of 1992 and February-March 1994. It is very interesting, the reading of these documents, because you can see a lot of decisions, rules, regulations, approved/published in order to establish the complete control over the area by HVO and Herceg-Bosna. I mean, in these 300 pages, you can find a new regulation, fiscal regulation, the appointment of commissions and governments; you can find the decision to dismantle the university, the Muslim university, Dzemal Bijedic -- the university, sorry, devoted to a Muslim personality, Dzemal Bijedic. It was the University of Mostar, and 4 another university was created, the Croat University of Mostar, which is -- sorry, this is of interest peculiar because I am professor -- the Rector was appointed by the HVO and was responsible to the HVO for his actions, so no autonomy at all. Then you can find several other decisions. For instance, about the complete educational system, even the certificates, the insignia, the ranks of the army. So it's a very interesting list of decisions that -- you can find also, this is very interesting, in addition the decision that made the Croat currency the currency of Herceg-Bosna, and the decision of 1993 where it was established that the air space of Herzegovina was under the control of the Croat Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And is there any other evidence of the role that Croatia played in the military and political life of Herceg-Bosna which you can refer us to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there are other elements. An important role was played since the beginning of the war in Bosnia, I mean, since the beginning of April 1992, by General Janko Bobetko. General Janko Bobetko is a very famous person, very well known in Croatia, because he was Tito's General, as Tudjman was. During the second half of the '60s, the beginning of the '70s, he supported the nationalistic claims in Croatian Zagreb, and for this reason he was charged with nationalism by Tito and for this reason he was expelled from political life after 1971. He, after 1990, when Communism collapsed, he came back on the political/military scene and he became, in 1991, a military advisor of the Presidency and the Government of Croatia. Then on April 10, he was sent as Chief-of-Staff to the southern front to manage the southern front of Croatia because he had excellent results, military results, in outcomes during 1992. At the end of the year, in fall 1992, he came back to Zagreb and became Chief-of-Staff of the Croat army. He prepared, under his command there were prepared the most successful operations of the Croat army when they -- to recover control of Peruca, of Maslenica Bridge, and even the Oluja offensive was prepared under his command, albeit he retired in 1995 becoming member of the Sabor, of the Croat parliament. He wrote very interesting memoirs published 0011 in Zagreb in 1996 in which he reconstructs the battles during the wars. The book is entitled "Svemojebitke," "All My Battles," and he published a lot of documents in this book. You know why southern front was so important for Croatia and why Croatia was so interested, at least, in controlling one part of Bosnia? There are many reasons. I mentioned yesterday historical reasons, but more practical reasons were of greater interest to the Croatian government between January and April 1992. That is, in -- may I just show you the map of Bosnia in order to help? You can come back again to one of the maps. Maybe one of the -- this can be interesting. Map 114 is of the 1918, but it allows one to see better the borders between -- so the map 114.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you need to press the button. You may have it on your screen now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah. It's good because you can see the borders, and the borders of Bosnia and Croatia haven’t change since 1918. I don't have in --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If you press "Video" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The video is the second button down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Now is. And as you can see, particularly Dubrovnik because it was bombed in the fall 1991. It was under the risk of bombardment by the Serbs from the area of Tribja, this area behind Dubrovnik. So it was very important for Croatia to have -- at least a guarantee that this area will not be under the bombardment of the Serbs. So for this reason, they were interested in having control of the southern part of Herceg-Bosna in order to defend, to defend the southern part of Dalmatia and the Dubrovnik area. This was one reason. The other reason was, of course, that there were many -- there was the agreement. I spoke yesterday of this agreement with Milosevic in Karajordjevo in 1991 and then the following actions taken by the government -- by Tudjman or by the Herceg-Bosna government in order to ease the relationships between these two parts of Croatia. One can take into consideration, I mentioned the decision of Herceg-Bosna to accept and to introduce the currency, the Croat currency in Herceg-Bosna, the control of the air space given to Croatia. Or even we can mention the maps; very often by the newspaper, the journalists considered prepared by Tudjman himself. One of the incidents particularly happened in London in 1995 when, if you remember it was in all the newspapers, when a map of Bosnia was drawn and the journalists claimed it was made personally Tudjman who prepared this map in this restaurant and where the partition of Bosnia was very clear, and Banja Luka was assigned to Croatia. Banja Luka is a predominantly Serb city. While Tuzla, which is predominantly a Muslim city, was assigned to Serbia. So the division was in this sense. Otherwise, otherwise, you know in addition that since 1995, the Croat government has granted 10 percent of the seats in the Sabor, in the Croatian parliament, to the -- formally the Croat Diaspora. This 10 percent of seats were occupied by representatives from Herceg-Bosna, so they took part in the elections in Croatia in 1995 and can do so in the years to come. So this is a very peculiar situation even in the international context.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just touching on that point there --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just touching on that point you just mentioned about the seats in the Croatian Sabor. Are you saying that when there are elections in Croatia that those elections spill over into Bosnia-Herzegovina 0014 and that 10 percent of the parliament is devoted to Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, yes, 10 percent of the seats. And then I can mention even the recent -- just to give you a trend. The recent, in 1997, proposal again coming from Tudjman to create a confederation between Croatia and the Federation of Bosnia. This means the Federation established by the United States in 1994 with the Washington agreement between the Muslims and the Croats. So in this -- this -- you know, when -- every time when -- the proposal arrives from Croatia to create a confederation with the Bosnian Federation, it creates a lot of concern and sensitivity in Bosnia, particularly within the Muslim population but also within those who claim, democrats who claim the sovereignty and integrity of the whole of Bosnia. So you have -- even you had in Sarajevo press in second half of 1997 strong reactions against this proposal of Tudjman. So this is the context of the disputed relations between the government in Zagreb and the government in Sarajevo. But coming back again to Bobetko. Bobetko described in his memoirs his meeting with Gojko Susak on April 10th. He went to Susak and he explained to him how important it was to create a southern command in order to protect Dubrovnik and Dalmatia. Gojko Susak agreed with him, and both of them went to Tudjman. Tudjman immediately appointed Janko Bobetko as head or chief of the southern command, and thanks to this, he started his action in southern Dalmatia. So this was also a way just to confirm that decisions were made on the top of the government between particularly -- direct contacts with the President of the Republic and the Minister of Defence when it involved this part of the former Yugoslavia. And this can explain probably why the HVO in the end was considered dependent upon the headquarters in Split where Janko Bobetko was the chief commander. The OSCE published a table, a map you have in exhibit number 117. This document is in two pages, and I will explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps you might tell us first where it comes from, if you would? It doesn't seem to be working properly. Put it on video --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The document is in two pages only because I wanted to make clear the other one just to offer you to see in the page where the table was. It was on the first half of the page. And then in the other you have just a larger picture in order to see better the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you got the document from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The document is -- the map was included in the confidential document of OSCE prepared last year, and as I mentioned before when I spoke about the relations between Gojko Susak, Miroslav Tudjman, and the private enterprise Alan, it was included in this document, and this document has been published by the magazine Dani in Sarajevo. So this map has been included in this document, and you can see in this annex first the organisation of the Croat army, and this is the first -- the first picture. The second one, you have the picture of the HVO, the HVO army, Croat Defence Council command, how they were organised, and then you have the relation, the general staff in the third of the Croat army with the different district, Osijek, Bjelovar, Zagreb, and Karlovac, and then you have the Corps District 6 in Split, and from this you have the HVO general staff under this command. So in the Corps District 6 was acting Bobetko, and then you have this connection, direct connection, between HVO general staff and the Corps District 6 of Split linked to the general staff of Croatia who was under the control of Bobetko from fall in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And it says down at the very bottom "HV-HVO Integrated Command Structure For Wartime Combat Operations." What particular period of time does this relate to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for Bobetko is the period between April 1992 and fall 1992, but then, then this relations -- and we have documents on this continued in the months to come, in 1993, so -- and in 1994, so as we can see from the evidence of international documents, not only from documents coming from the battlefields.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that the time frame really for this is from '92 through to '94?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what about the other document on the second page? What's the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The second page of that document, what is the significance of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second page of this document is just to make clear for the Court because it is the same document but -- in the first you see where in the page of the magazine was the table and then just to clarify, to better clarify, to allow you to read better, yes, because otherwise, it was very complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were the political measures taken by Croatia in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean in this sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, during the period of the conflict, starting right at the beginning and going through to 1995, what political steps were taken by Croatia in relation to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But, you know, I mentioned the economic support to the -- the support came particularly from the Ministry of Defence. I have documents on this economic support, and if the Court allows, I can refresh my memory and I can give details on documents on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Just tell us in general terms what it is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, in general terms it was, for instance, documents referring that 540,000 Deutschmark were offered to Bugojno in order to defend themselves or they send, even from the Minister of Defence, support 10,000 Deutschmark to the HDZ of one area in Bosnia. So it was economic support that arrived or before -- even on the eve of the war, March '92, or even when the war erupted after, so there were documents in this sense that confirmed this kind of economic support coming directly from the Ministry of Defence, particularly. Sometimes Ministry of Finance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Moving on to exhibit 118, which is the next document that you have there before you, what's the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1918, you mention?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, document 118.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have another one, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It's the next document --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I have organised differently and so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It's not 19.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. Ah, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, no, no. The document I'm referring to, Professor, is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: -- the "Conclusions of The Joint Meeting of the Herzegovina Regional Meeting and the Travnik Regional Community."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is the number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eighteen?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Eighteen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Eighteen. 118.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well ... Yes, yes. This is the Serbo Croat version, and this -- the regional, and this is the translation of the document. Let me say that this is a very interesting document, but this document is connected with a peculiar phase, a phase before the beginning of the war. We are in November 1991. And in order to understand this document, it should be interesting to refer to another document, another document that has been -- this is the minutes of a meeting that took place in Travnik and where Dario Kordic participated, where the representative in Herceg-Bosna in this area made pressure and outlined the possibility to reschedule differently the policy of HDZ. We have to take into account that at that time Stjepan Klujic was still the President of HDZ. And in this document, people, the Croat representative in Herceg-Bosna, spoke about the risk of a silent occupation that was going on. In fact, a silent occupation that was going on in Bosnia, this was in July of 1991, and for this reason they supported a more aggressive political attitude of HDZ. They charged the representative of HDZ in the Bosnian parliament to be puppets of the SDA, the party of Izetbegovic, and for this reason they claimed the creation of a kind of regional Croat organisation of Herceg-Bosna. This was in July 1991, and only in November was Herceg-Bosna established. So this showed the current stream within the HDZ was preparing a different political orientation than that of Stjepan Klujic at the moment, and this explained why, in February 1992, Klujic was overthrown. After this meeting in July 1991, we had a second meeting, this document, in November, the 12th of November, 1991. This document --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: "This document" is exhibit --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The exhibit now, under the number 118 and 118a, little (a), the letterhead is of the Croat Democratic Union, is a document with the Conclusions of a Joint Meeting of the Herzegovina Regional Community and the Travnik Regional Community, and it is followed -- it was signed by Boban and Kordic and is followed by a list of about 22 names, people who write -- who wrote their signatures. What is interesting about this document, if you consider particularly the conclusion, the conclusion informed us that meetings took place in Zagreb with President Franjo Tudjman on 13 and 20 June, 1991, that is before the war erupted in Yugoslavia, before the proclamation of independence of Slovenia and Croatia. And if you read after "Proceeding from these conclusions adopted at the aforementioned meetings" in Grude in October 1991, in Busovaca in October 1991, that is in two towns of Bosnia, "these two regional communities jointly and unanimously," that is, the Herzegovina Regional Community and the Travnik Regional Community, "these two regional communities jointly and unanimously decided that the Croat people in Bosnia and Herzegovina must finally start conducting a decisive and active policy which should bring about the realisation of our eternal dream - a joint Croat State." I think that we don't need to comment on this sentence if you think also about the maps we spoke of yesterday, the historical dream, the eternal dream, you can understand very well this claim, which is supported in this sentence immediately after when it is speaking, about three lines after: "... (the proclamation of Croat banovina ..." "Banovina" means "immediately," and if you have memory of yesterday, you can remember very well why the use of this term. "... the Croatian banovina in Bosnia-Herzegovina." So a kind of autonomous area in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then to "conduct a referendum for joining the Republic of Croatia." So the first step was the creation of an autonomous area under the control, it's clear, of the Croat leadership, and then to conduct a referendum. If you think what happened later, when I mentioned all the laws, regulations, orders, published in the official gazette between 1992 and 1994, as I referred earlier, you can see how this decision was implemented in the years to come. Then, if you go to the point 2 of the same document, you can find: "Among some of the leaders of the HDZ for Bosnia and Herzegovina there are still forces which oppose these historical interests of the Croat people in Bosnia and Herzegovina." I think that we can read immediately the name Stjepan Klujic because of what I said. So "oppose these historical interests," and again you can see is mentioned the word "history." So this sentence is : "These forces are in favour of non-existent sovereign Bosnia." You see? Just to make clear the reference to Klujic because he defended southern Bosnia. And then in the end of the same sentence, you can find the sentences -- "We must show" -- the three lines at the end: "We must show Europe and the world which areas are the Croat areas in Bosnia and Herzegovina and where our future lies. These people will on no account accept any other solution except within the borders of a free Croatia." So I think that this is also sentence, this is very clear, so the perspective is to create a common state with Croatia, with Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, Professor, conversely, was there any provision in the constitution of Croatia of 1990 which would have facilitated the incorporation of Croat people living in other states?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If you read the Constitution, basic sources, point 1 at the beginning of the Constitution, you can find a very interesting sentence, when the Croat Republic was defined. And so it's written that the Croat Republic was established as the national state of the Croat people. So the national state of the Croat people. It is a clear aspect of the ethnic orientation of the State of Croatia, which is supported, in fact, by the Article 10, second paragraph, of the same constitution, where it is written that part of the Croat people living abroad, part of the Croat people living abroad -- it is very interesting because again you have a collective dimension of the rights of an ethnic group. This part of the Croat people will receive support, special support from the Croat State. So this is a duty that the constitution gives to the Croat state in order to protect the part of the people outside -- living abroad, which means particularly the area of Herceg-Bosna so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And in your researches, did you discover any evidence of duality of citizenship, any documents or material that supported dual citizenship between Croatia and Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. If I can refer to the document -- exhibit document 121 in "A," 121 A -- sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 126. Yes. 126, yes. 126. Here. I found it. First I would like to draw your attention to the document, the decision recognising the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign independent state signed by the President of the Croat Republic, Franjo Tudjman, in Zagreb the 7th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What document number is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's document 126 B.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why did you want to draw attention to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is very interesting if you take into consideration particularly the second paragraph of point 1: "International recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall imply that the Croat people, as one of the three constituent nations in Bosnia and Herzegovina, shall be guaranteed their sovereign rights." So in a sense it makes clear that the recognition is directly linked to the fact that the sovereign rights of the Croat people in Bosnia will be granted in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the second is the point 2 where it is written that: "This act of recognition grants the right to dual citizenship to the members of the Croat nation who wish citizenship. Furthermore, we wish to propose that this issue be regulated by a bilateral agreement." This agreement in this case -- in the case the Croatia started to send application forms for -- for --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Citizenship.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- citizenship immediately, and I have evidence of 2,000 forms -- more than 2,000 forms sent to Mostar to be distributed to the population. So it was not that one single citizen went to the Embassy or the Representative of the Croatian State abroad and asked for dual citizenship providing documents, but application forms were sent immediately by -- through the Mostar representative of Herceg-Bosna to the population in order to encourage the population to ask for dual citizenship. Anyway, if you consider also document 126 A, exhibit 126 A, you can see this is the document of -- this document is of September 1992, is a document of Herceg-Bosna, of the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna. It was published in the official gazette and is a decision about the creation -- a later publication of the document approved in November. As you see, at the end of the document you see the date, Mostar, 18 November, 1991, at the end of the document there the signature of President of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban. But it was published in the gazette, in the official gazette in September 1992 because they didn't have an official gazette before. So in this document you can see also an element of not complete adherence to the idea of the sovereignty and independence of Bosnia. If you look at point 2, paragraph 2 of the reasons: "Through their party, the Croatian Democratic Union and the legally elected government in this Republic, Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina have supported a sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina but always emphasised that they are protecting their own historical area and the interests of the entire Croat people." Which means that they had a very close image of their own territory which they were protecting, this historical area and the interests of the entire Croat people. This is the entire Croat people, which is something ambiguous considering that "entire" can take into consideration also the Croat people outside Bosnia-Herzegovina. And then is very interesting also the sentence, you can see in the third paragraph. You know, when we speak about self-determination generally, we speak about self-determination, and you can find the document on self-determination, until, including, the right of secession. If you look here at the first -- the fifth, sixth line, it's very interesting, you can find --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, it might be better if you can point to the projector.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. It is here: "... inalienable and indivisible right the non-transferable and the non-expandable --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It has to be translated. You have to speak much slower; otherwise, the translators can't pick it up.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see here is the document on self-determination, the sovereignty of the people, including the right to associate, which is very interesting and strange because you have the right of secession. Here you have the right to associate. And it's clear that it means taking into consideration the documents we spoke before, "associate" means associate this area to Croatia. So if you think that the strategy was more or less a first step in having an area under the complete control of Croat authorities in Bosnia and then to link this area to Croatia, you can see in this document even elements of this policy supported and repeated. So this shows what went on before the war in Bosnia and in the phases immediately after the war erupted in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: It would be good to have a break now, Mr. Niemann. So we shall adjourn for a 20-minute break?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: All rise, please. --- Recess at 10.22 a.m. --- Resume at 10.47 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may start. I should, however, like to say a few words regarding the organisation of our work; namely, we shall be taking a break of 15 minutes around noon, at noon, and that's it. You may now proceed. Excuse me, I see that Mr. Aleksovski is not in court. Okay. Now you may start, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, during the course of your evidence this morning, you made reference to General Janko Bobetko, and I think you've included amongst your documents, in particular Exhibit 121A through to 121O documents that relate to General Bobetko. I'm wondering if, looking at those documents and preferably proceeding through them in order, you can take us through them and indicate to us what you see as the significance of them in relation to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina in '92-'93?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First, I prepared just a map. This is Exhibit No. 120, it's a map that was prepared here by the officials of the Tribunal under my direction. It shows the main cities, areas which were included or quoted in the documents or in the documents published by Janko Bobetko in his memoirs. I just added some of the main cities of Croatia and Bosnia, just to help you to locate all the areas of, for instance, Split, Srebrenica, Bihac, Banja Luka, Tuzla, of course just to give you the context, while the main area, the main area quoted is that which you see from Metkovic, Ploce to Miljacena, Prozor, Bugojno or Livno. This is the area which is of interest because of the military actions directed by General Janko Bobetko. So this is just the general picture, and we can come back to the map when something is not clear, just to locate the places. And then we can start looking at the documents. The first one is document 121.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's 121A I think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 121A is in English, yes. All these documents here relate to the actions of Bobetko -- the military actions of Bobetko on the southern front which were published in the book of Bobetko himself in Zagreb. This is a document with the letterhead of the Croat Republic, the President of the Republic. It is an order on the basis of which General Bobetko was appointed commander of all the units of the Croatian army on the southern front, from Split to Dubrovnik. That is in the area that I quoted before. This is just to show you the order that the Croatian navy was under his command and he was also authorised to recruit staff for his activities because it was non-existent at the time. This is the first document. Then we have a series of documents related to the decisions made by Janko Bobetko during military operations in 1992. The first one is the No. 121B. This document is a document with the letterhead of the Commander of Split operative zone, as you can see, the Ploce forward command post. Ploce is on the coast -- on the Adriatic Sea. It is an order sent by the commander of the Split operative zone on the basis of the ordinance of General Janko Bobetko. And what is particularly interesting is point 2 in Citluk, make contact with Mr. Perak, the Defence commander of that part of Herzegovina, and coordinate the defence of that area with him. Citluk is in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this is just the first order to establish coordination of the defence between Herceg-Bosna and Croatia. And what is interesting is particularly point 6, 6-6, you see it is -- the original was like this, "All HV...", this is Croatian army, hard to be removed from the fighters and present yourselves as volunteer defenders of your homeland." Let me say that this is significant enough, I think. I found, and I had an opportunity to see several documents, not only one, with this sentence included for whole period 1992-1993. Documents from Tomislovgrad, from Livno, or documents from Vitez, in which you can find this statement based on the HVO order and on that from the commander of Split. As you can see in this document, soldiers, officers of the Croatian army had to remove their insignia, and the order in these documents clarifies that this was because this could create trouble for Croatia on the international scene. So this was -- it was very clear. It is written in these documents, please inform the soldiers, explain the reasons, but it's better if they don't have enough identity cards or insignia of HVO to be put instead of the HV, of the Croatian army, it is better not to have any insignia. So this was the suggestion, it was better not to have insignias at all. In fact, there are many documents that can confirm this relationship even on other aspects as, for instance, connections with the problem of the military service recruits who had the opportunity to do their military service in Bosnia. This was as in Croatia; that is, there was an exchange, a kind of an agreement that people doing their military service in Bosnia were exempt in Croatia and vice versa. Or there were even changes in the military. You remember the document of Gojko Susak I mentioned before. There are other people who, for instance, received the rank of colonel in Herceg-Bosna. They were given a certificate so that they could continue their activities in declaration army, moving from HVO, from the Herceg-Bosna army to the Croatian army. So anyway, this point 6 is very interesting for this reason, because it made clear that in April, 1992 -- but this sentence was repeated very often in other documents, as I told you, this -- it was very clear that there were concerns in the international community about the involvement of Croatia in Bosnia. And this is the reason why it was suggested to the officials and soldiers of the Croatian army to leave off the insignia of the Croatian army. Then we can see the following document, document No. 121C. This is a very interesting document. If you look at the letterhead, the letterhead is Southern Front Command. Then immediately Southern Front Command, the line immediately after is "Followed command post Grude," but Grude is not in Croatia, it is in Bosnia. And then what is interesting, if you look at the signature, the signature and the stamp is -- on the other page -- General Janko Bobetko, signed and stamped Herceg-Bosna, main staff. But Janko Bobetko was appointed by Tudjman as the chief commander for the southern front in Croatia, so you see that he used the stamp of Herceg-Bosna, main staff. So we can conclude that Janko Bobetko was the chief of both the Croatian army and the HVO at that time. The southern front included not only part of Croatia, but even Herzegovina, that is part of another state, that is, Bosnia-Herzegovina. And what is also interesting in this document is point 2 -- not only point 1 is the southern front to be established as the forward command post established in Grude. The second point is the responsible officer of the forward command post in my absence shall be Colonel Milivoj Petkovic who holds all authority as Colonel relating to the command and coordination of combat activities. Petkovic is very interesting figure in the sense that he was born in Dalmatia, in a village close to Sibenik. If you look at the map, Sibenik is here, and you can see where is Grude, because we were speaking, and Citluk, because we quoted also Citluk. He was born in a village close to Djibnic, he was a Croat, he became general after this. He was now -- you see in this document, he was appointed by Bobetko to be responsible on his behalf for the forward command post Grude, but then he became a general, the head, the chief of the staff of HVO. He was later the head of the command of the HVO and then he came back to Croatia, as a general in the Croatian army. So he is an interesting person for this reason alone. We can go further and see the document, the following document, 121D. We are now again in the -- with this document in the Republic of Croatia southern front command, as you can see from the letterhead. What is interesting in this letter is, first -- the first point: Major General Roso, is to immediately strengthen the command staff of Tomislovgrad - Tomislovgrad is in Bosnia. You can see Tomislovgrad is here - and use his influence and most energetic action towards all groups and individuals who wish to promote their sense to commanders of various layouts. So it is said to make order in this area. And then in point No. 4, the commander of the forward military post, Milivoj Petkovic shall be at the disposal of Tomislovgrad command until further notice and he was replaced. So Bobetko, decided who has to go and make order in one area of Bosnia, who had to move from one part to another part. And this is also interesting, the last point, where it is written there: RH, that is the Republic of Croatia, Minister of Defence, that means Gojko Susak, shall be notified immediately about the situation in Tomislovgrad, as about the situation in Bosnia, and be asked to visit that town as soon as possible, please, and be asked to visit that town as soon as possible and to use his authority to eliminate all groups and individuals who claim to answer directly to the Minister. So it was clearly an attempt probably to work outside the order of Bobetko and he wanted, because he had the agreement with Susak, as you remember, in April, 1992 before going to Tudjman about his activities, and he wanted to have the influence of Minister Susak in Tomislovgrad in order to make clear that who is the chief and the commander in the whole area. And so it's interesting because Gojko Susak is asking to come to Bosnia as soon as possible and to use his influence to control this part of the Herceg-Bosna authorities -- local authorities. This confirms more about the strong links between Gojko Susak and the Herzegovina authorities with a different point of view. I think that we can go forward to the document 121E. This document again of the Republic of Croatia is a document of 19 May, 1992, from -- the letterhead is again the Republic of Croatia, Bobetko signed as Republic of Croatia, Croatian army command, and what is interesting is the first point, for instance: "Establish a forward command post in Central Bosnia in Gornji Vakuf. You can see where is Gornji Vakuf on the map; you can see it is in the heart of Bosnia here, close to the heart of Bosnia. So it is not only as the first time, Capljina, Grude, Citluk, Grude, now in Gornji Vakuf. So Bobetko made the decision from a letterhead of the Croatian Republic who he has had to be the forward command post in Central Bosnia, and not only he created this -- the forward command post, but he appointed, as you see in the point 2, Brigadier Jakupovic as the commander of the forward command post. Then we can go further, document 121F. You see this is also a military order. This is a military order sent by Bobetko as a commander of the southern front with the letterhead of Croatia, from Ploce. This is a document of 15 June, 1992. And it's very interesting to turn our attention to the end of the point 1 when explaining about the enemy - in at the end you can see the sentence, reinforcement of two tanks has been sent toward Cobanovo Polje from the direction of Nevesimje for psychological effect." If you look at the map again, you can see where Nevesimje is. So you can see the area of action is this wide area of Herzegovina and Central Bosnia. In the same document you can find, again at the point 2.1, quoted what HVO has to do in Capljina, the Capljina compromising the tanks, shall organise active defence in its zone of responsibility, and so on and so on at this point. You can see. And if you turn the page, page 2, you can see again quoted, tanks from Capljina HVO should go as support to the area of Pileta. This was again the area of Capljina which is close to the border here, it's part of Bosnia. Close to Medjugorje and Pocitelj, this area. We can go further? Yeah. So the number now 121G.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And if the document just reconfirms the previous points--

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --just say so, and we can move more quickly through them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is another interesting document. The document is, as you can see from the letterhead, Republic of Croatia, southern front command, dated April 19 and is done in Grude, that is in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And it's just Exhibit 121G.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And if you look at the signature at the end, the document is signed and stamped again by General Bobetko as a commander of the southern front with the stamp of the Herceg-Bosna main staff. So with the stamp of a region in another state. And in this document, you can turn your attention in particular to the order, to point one, where it's written immediately begin to prepare for and recognise the crucial defence in Livno and Tomislovgrad. If you look again at the map, you can see Livno and Tomislovgrad are in Bosnia. So all the area -- you see, again, the area under the control of Vakuf, Nevesimje, Livno, Capljina, Citluk, this was the area, again confirmed by the document. The next exhibit is No. 121H.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is of April. This is a document of April, 1992, letterhead Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, again southern front command, Grude, Grude foreign post again. So you can see this southern front was not only a front in Croatia but consisted of a wider front including parts of another state. This is clear. You can see here just a list of people appointed by General Bobetko as a commanders of the different HVO units, of the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna. These are officers, I found their names very often, especially of Zegko Sigec, who was particularly involved in a question connected to the citizenship and documents related to 1993, information about the need of leaving off the insignia of the Croatian army from soldiers -- officers and soldiers of the Croatian army acting in Bosnia. This is just to give you an idea of the list of persons. You see commanders, deputy commanders, chiefs, captains, administrative offices, chiefs of artillery. So it's large -- chiefs of communication, chiefs of engineering, lieutenants, chiefs of intelligence. It's a large group of persons with different responsibilities who were appointed by Bobetko himself. Okay. We can go further. This now, turn to document 121I. This is interesting. If you look, even the original document, you can see the letterhead of the -- and you have the translation of the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna of HVO and you can see that, in spite of this kind of letterhead, you have the signature of the commander of the southern front again, Janko Bobetko, with the stamp of Herceg-Bosna. And again this is the appointment of major general Ante Roso responsible for the Livno region. Livno is another town in Bosnia, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I think there is also a reference there to the Prozor Konjic region as well in the second paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Konic, yes. Konic is a town, a town to the north of Mostar, along the River Neretva. The River Neretva, Mostar is going to Jablanica and Konic which is more or less here, and then you leave the Neretva, the course of Neretva and you go straight to -- the road goes straight to Sarajevo. You can consider Konic is more or less here after Jablanica and Mount Prajnia, in this area. So this is. We can go further. Document 121J again, I mean, this is new confirmation -- this is another document of April, as you see the date is April 21st, which is three, four weeks after the beginning of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The official one. You can see that the document is again with the letterhead Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, HVO, southern front command, and the signature is General Janko Bobetko and signed with the staff -- Herceg-Bosna staff. So this is another document which confirms that Janko Bobetko was managing military actions of HVO in the period. Can we go further. Yes. The following document is number 121K. This is an interesting document, again for the following reasons: This is a document done in Ploce, that is in Croatia. You can see 4th May, 1992, the Republic of Croatia southern front command, and is signed by Janko Bobetko. The signature is as a commander of the southern front in the framework of the Croatian State. And what is interesting in the order is that preparation and submission of a list of future operation of -- this is, you see, the anti-tank system, against the JNA. 60 people were to be designed -- were to come from HVO headquarters of Herceg-Bosna, and the preoccupation of the General is that all the units of HVO should be equally represented. So he gave a very clear order to train or to prepare future operations involving all the units of HVO. We can go further. The following exhibit is 121 -- yes, the following is 121L. Again, we have a document -- this is a document of June 14, and the letterhead is once again Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. You see it concerns on the period April-May. You can find letters with the letterhead of the Croatian Republic or of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna indifferently, and Bobetko signed here with the stamp of Herceg-Bosna again. And in this letter, he is giving an order to prepare military identity cards for the members of HVO units. This explains why these military cards were a problem. Sometimes they didn't have enough military identity cards for the soldiers in 1993. That's why, in the document I mentioned, and which we had an opportunity to see, it was written sometimes at the end of 1992, beginning of 1993, the first month of 1993 that in the event that soldiers or officials of the Croatian army had no military identity card of HVO, it was better to participate in the fighting without any insignia but not with the insignia of the Croatian army. This is just the beginning of a story, this lecture, yes. So we can go further. This is 121. The following is 121M. This is a document of the Croatian Republic sent from Ploce on July 13, 1992, and is an order to the operative groups in south-eastern Herzegovina, operating in south-eastern Herzegovina, It is a document that included order for defence around Mostar. I can confirm that in his memoirs, when he wrote them, Janko Bobetko explained clearly that the so-called Cagal operation - that is Jackal in English - ended with, and he explained that Mostar was freed by the Croat army and HVO jointly. So the operation was -- this was because there were many, many disputes later between HVO and the Bosnian army. The Bosnian army charged HVO with having participated in the liberation of Mostar with another army of another State, not under an international or bilateral agreement between Bosnia and Croatia, and even an army that acted later in cooperation with HVO against the sovereign independence of Bosnia in an operation against the Muslims. So this was one of the elements of the disputes during 1993 and the beginning of 1994 before signing the Washington Agreement which stopped the war between the Muslims and the Croats in Bosnia. The agreement was signed in 1994, March. It was imposed by the United States. This is the interest of this document. We can continue. 121N. This is another document of orders of General Bobetko from June, 1992 related to -- and the letter is -- the document is with a letterhead of the Republic of Croatia, signed by Bobetko in -- as a commander of the Croatian army, and what is of interest is particularly the end of the document here -- no. Where it is written point 3 -- point 1: "Forces of the Mostar HVO shall move toward another area." So that is, you see, another document which confirms that the orders for operational activities to be carried out by HVO were coming directly from General Bobetko And on the other pages, point 3, point 2, you can see that the Stolac battalion in Celpatur captured the Stolac region. If you look again at the map of Bosnia, you can see where Stolac is. It is in this part of Herzegovina, the south-eastern part of Herzegovina. We can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the next document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the next -- the next document is the last one, 121O. It's a document of June 18. Again, a document -- a document of the Republic of Croatia, this is the letterhead, and signed directly by Bobetko, the pages, and there you can find several quotations of the activities that had to be done in the area. For instance, south-western Herzegovina immediately -- to move immediately from Medjugorje to Mostar. This is what he contributed to in the liberation of Mostar in 1992. You can see that he assigned a zone of responsibility and made each unit responsible for its assigned zone. You can see also -- all the document is connected, as you can see, at the beginning, immediately after detention of and of. Following the liberation of the east bank of the Neretva river and the city of Mostar in order to establish the order of battle along the achieved lines fully controlling -- and so on and so on. So it was liberating Mostar, giving orders to continue and to operate in other areas which you see in other points, point 4, for instance, Stolac, HVO. Other orders including and involving HVO and coming again from General Bobetko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, did this close working relationship between the HVO and the HV continue on through 1993- 94?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did there occur in the latter part of 1992 an increase in tension between the forces of the HVO-HV and the forces of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Tensions -- tensions which were even reported by journalists. It is an interesting exercise to follow the newspapers, international or local ones, about the evolution of the war in Bosnia. And there is evidence of clashes, particularly in the area around, as you can see, I can use this map which can help, in the area Travnik and Novi Travnik already in October and September -- October and November 1992 in Prozor, then in Vitez. So these three areas, that is areas in the so-called Central Bosnia, there were troubles and clashes between the Muslims and Croats in that period. It's interesting that on October 9th I found in newspapers information that the Minister of Defence of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, announced a cease-fire, a joint cease-fire between the Serb armies and the Bosnian army. And what is interesting is the comment of the newspapers in the sense that the newspapers referred to that for the first time, and they stressed this, this was the first time that Croatian army was doing something without the Muslims. This cease-fire was a cease-fire, according to the newspapers, only between the Croats and the Serbs, excluding, in this sense, the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I think that in the transcript it says that the agreement was between the Serb armies and the Bosnian army. I don't think you meant Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serb army of Bosnia, yes, yes, the Serb Republic of -- the Serb Republic of Bosnia, Herceg-Bosna. So it was between two armies, the Serb army in Bosnia and Herceg-Bosna, Bosnian army, HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: To be distinguished from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, distinguished army of Herceg-Bosna so yes, because sometimes the Muslim army, sometimes the army of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe to us the development of these tensions that existed between the Muslims and the Croats in Bosnia in 1993 -- 1992, leading through to 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: '93, yes. You know, in the -- at the end of 1992, Vance and Owen were received -- well, requested to prepare a plan, a possible plan to be submitted to the parties in conflict, and this plan was submitted in Geneva at the beginning of January, 1993. May I refer to the map in Exhibit No. 119? This is the map of the Vance-Owen Plan. The Vance-Owen Plan was Exhibit 119. The plan was organised in such -- articulated in such a way that Bosnia was confirmed as an independent and sovereign state based on 10 cantons, and Bosnia was divided, the map was suggesting into different cantons. These 10 cantons were divided in such a way that three were under the predominance of Croats, three under the predominance of Serbs, three under the predominant of the Muslims, and one, Sarajevo district, for all of them together. So you can see from this map the areas 3, 8, 10 were assigned to the Croatian area, you see this is the area of Herceg-Bosna, more or less, and this is the area of Posnija.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And, Professor, did the presentation of this plan to some extent tend to support the aspirations of the Croats and the Serbs in relation to Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As you can see also the -- in a way, yes. Because, as I mentioned, the first war goal of both Croats and Serbs was the establishment of an area completely under their own control and then to prepare the association with the borders. We have also a document from the Serb side which is more or less similar to that of -- we had seen from the meeting in Grude on November 12, 1991. The Serb document is a document published of a meeting with a brigade, of a brigade following another meeting which took place in Banja Luka in 1992 when the war had already erupted in April -- erupted in Bosnia -- May, sorry, May 1992, May. It's important, May, because the document was written that some difficulties had arisen on the Serb side because Milosevic was compelled by the international community to withdraw one part of the military in order -- you remember the 20 percent, the cosmetic change of the activity of JNA in Bosnia, it was in that period. And so they met in Banja Luka, and in the brigades in order to clearly establish the war goals of the SDS and the Serb army. The war goals were in particular to set up an area completely under the control of the Serbs, to have the control of the borders between the river Una and Neretva, which means this border, but not to establish any border, any controlled border where Bosnia neighboured on the self-proclaimed Republic of Serb Krajina, this area. It was just to establish the border between Dalmatia, under the control of Croatia and Bosnia, but not in the area controlled by the Serbs in Croatia, because the idea was, in the end, to connect the two areas. As you can see, this was the proposal, the proposal of Vance- again stressing the idea that these cantons were predominantly ethnic cantons. This was the interpretation, effectively, of the Croat and Serb side, from the Croat and Serb side. For instance, this map was presented at the beginning of January, but we have a document of January -- if I well remember, 15 January. I had document with me, signed by the President of the HVO in which it was clearly stated that in cantons 3, 8, 9 assigned by the Vance-Owen Plan to the control of the Croat authorities, the authorities of Bosnian army, both -- Herzegovina army, had to submit to the command of HVO or leave the areas. And this order was followed by similar orders and requests by other heads of HVO units, for instance, immediately in Mostar, immediately in Konjic, that is in this area, in January 1993, and then in Travnik in April, 1993 when the troop of Dario Kordic -- in this period. You know, the state symbols had very great importance, flags, insignia. So formally the war erupted between -- in the night between the 7th and 8th of April, 1993. In order to follow this -- to accomplish the order of Prlic, the flags of the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna were put up the local municipalities, local official municipalities of Travnik. The army, the Bosnian army opposed this, and clashes started, the military clashes started, and then the situation precipitated and precipitated particularly in Central Bosnia, that is in this area -- may I refer again to this map? Maybe in this case even more clear. This area around Travnik, Novi Travnik, Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, Busovaca, this area in particularly. In this situation, this area in June and then in August-September the army -- the Bosnian army had very great military success, and this created a lot of problems for HVO. We have from that period documents and evidence of attempts by HVO in this area to establish contact with the Serb army. Even an order -- we have a document of the Serb army explaining that they received a request for weapons and -- from the Herceg-Bosnian army in order to fight against the Muslims. And then together the Serbs -- Serb army and the HVO tried -- besieged Zepce, for instance. So there were in that period, particularly in the summer of 1993, relations between the Serb army and HVO. It was the period when Mate Boban and Karadzic again met in Montenegro to discuss the idea of the partition of Bosnia. The war was particularly important, this area, because, of course, the army, the Bosnian army tried to create -- to divide the area under the control of Herceg-Bosna. As you can see, this was the area claimed, and so they wanted to block the homogenisation of this area. So the war particularly escalated in this area or along the Neretva, especially in Mostar. As you know, Mostar was divided into parts. In November, the bridge was destroyed. All these events are well known. This was in November, 1993, and in this period, particularly in the period when -- from the -- when the HVO was defeated at the beginning of the summer and then -- by the army in Central Bosnia. And at the end of the year rumours, discussions, impressions increased in the international community because a lot of information was arriving that, particularly after the defeat of the HVO in Central Bosnia, Croatia sent soldiers and officials of the Croat army into Bosnia in order to help HVO in that period. And this was a very dramatic period for the Croat army, Croat army in Bosnia, for Herceg-Bosna too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, I think, Professor, that leads us to the next point, and that is the involvement of the international community, particularly in relation to the reaction by the international community to the involvement of Croatia, the Republic of Croatia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I think that you have a number of documents which illustrate the increasing concern of the international community in relation to Croatia's involvement in Bosnia-Herzegovina there. Perhaps you might take us through those documents, illustrating by reference to the documents the points that you wish to make in connection with this increasing international concern of Croatia's involvement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. So let us start with a document, Exhibit No. 122. This document is a document from the United Nations Security Council. It's a document dated the 30 May, 1992, and is connected with -- is a report of the Secretary-General pursuant to paragraph 4 of the Security Council Resolution 752. One had to report about several questions, several things connected to Bosnia. What is interesting for our discussion here now is particularly point No. 10 on the third page where it is stated, point 10 at the bottom of the page: "As regards." This is a point connected to the withdrawal of elements of the Croat army in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bear in mind the document is of May, 1992. This is connected with the Bobetko operations as I illustrated before. As regards withdrawal of elements of the Croat army. So it is clear the international community was aware of this. Now, in Bosnia-Herzegovina information currently available in New York suggests that no such withdrawal has occurred. UNPROFOR has received reliable reports of the Croatian army personnel in uniform operating within and as part of military formations in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Croatian authorities have consistently taken the position that the Croatian soldiers in Bosnia and Herzegovina have left the Croatian army and are not subject to its authority. International observations do not however doubt that portions of Bosnia and Herzegovina are under the control of Croatian military units, whether belonging to the local Territorial Defence, paramilitary groups, or to the Croatian army. It is unclear in the circumstances how their withdrawal or dismantlement as required by the council can be achieved." So if you take into consideration the documents we had the opportunity to see before and to make a connection, at the time they didn't have -- the international community didn't have the documents, we had the opportunity to read before. But as you can see through the representative of UNPROFOR, they received enough information to know that the soldiers or officers of the Croat army were there, all were there without their insignia, as you can see, particularly thinking on the last sentences of this point. You can make comparison, immediate comparison with another document. I am following differently the order, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Give us the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The number is 126C -- this is 122. 126C. This is resolution 752. Because this was quoted here in the beginning of this document. This is why I think that it's important. Resolution 752.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If you just place it on the screen, we can follow it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, resolution 752 (1992). This is the resolution of -- approved by the Security Council in May 1993 -- 15 May, 1993 -- in 1992, sorry, 1992. This 7 resolution is interesting, particularly point 3 on the following page where it's written, as you can see: "Demands that all forms of interference from outside Bosnia-Herzegovina including by units of the Yugoslav People's Army, JNA, as well as elements of the Croatian army cease immediately and the Bosnia-Herzegovina neighbours take swift actions to end such interference and respect the territorial integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina." This was the document written 15 days before the document I read previously; this was from document 122 and was a report on the basis of this request of -- coming from the Security Council and the Secretary-General reported the sentence -- point 10 I read a few minutes ago. It's also interesting, if we can go to another document, 126D now, D. Yes. This is another resolution of the Security Council. The resolution is number 787 of 1992, 16 November. Bobetko was at that time already Chief-of-Staff of the whole Croatian army, the southern front, in Zagreb, and the point -- the interesting point is the second -- after point 5 on the third page. This part where you can see about -- it's again a point on the form of interference and you can see after the resolution where it is quoted, resolution 752 (1992) and other relevant resolution, including the requirement that all forces, in particular elements of the Croat army -- you see, in particular elements. This now is particular. Before you had both, now you have particularly elements of Croatian army should be withdrawn or be subject to the authority of the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or be disbanded or disarmed. So the request was to take different -- or in any case to put this army under the control of the Republic of Bosnia, or to disarm or disband it, in any case to withdraw the Croatian army particularly from this -- from the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We can go further and see another document, especially document 126E. 126E. This is interesting because I spoke and I showed two documents and two resolutions of the Security Council. This is different. So United Nations, this is a document, a different document, it's a document of the European Council on Croatia. When the European Union had a meeting in Edinburgh at the end of December of 1992. We are following in this case the two resolutions of the United Nations, and you can 7 turn your attention particularly to the last sentences of point 2 on this page, last sentences here, where you can read the last four sentences: "The European Council calls on the Croatian authorities for their part to comply with all UN Security Council resolutions and to cooperate in good faith with the peace process, since they too carry a share of the responsibility for attacks on the Muslim population." Please consider that this is -- attacks on the Muslim population. This is December 1992. As I mentioned, the official war between Croats and Muslims started in April, 1993. As a consequence -- as a consequence of the Vance-Owen Plan but, as I mentioned before, clashes already started in September, October, and November. They stopped in the middle of November in the area of Central Bosnia, Travnik, Novi Travnik and Vitez. So this is a concern in this case of the European council about clashes already started in Central Bosnia and without any relation -- at the beginning there were events, the war started later, so there were concerns already about a situation that was growing on dramatically towards dramatic outcomes that happened later in 1993. So...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You can do another document, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Another document? Okay. We can see the following document is document 126F. We are coming again to the United Nations with this document. Was interesting, this document. This is a letter sent to the United Nations, the original is in English, it was sent on the 26th April, 1993. April 1993, it means that 20 days after the Travnik events that provoked the war between the Croats and Muslims. And this letter was sent by the -- by the permanent representative of Croatia to the United Nations to inform the United Nations that a common agreement had been found between Muslims and Croats. And what is interesting is the end of this document, on the third page, where you can see that the joint statement about coordination of the army, cooperation between the Croats and the Muslims, was signed by Izetbegovic and Mate Boban, the two of the Bosnian state with witnessed by Tudjman, the president of Croatia. So the president of Croatia in a way supported this moment and was the witness of this agreement between two parties of the same state. It's again confirmation that Mate Boban worked with the support of Franjo Tudjman. But if you see, the other page after, which is also interesting, the second document where it was established that the HVO has a representative in the command of the army, of the Bosnian army, of the Bosnian army, as a part of the Bosnian army, this document was signed by Izetbegovic and Boban as political representatives of the two parties signing the agreement, Muslims and the Croats, by General Milivoj Petkovic who was the general of the high command of the Bosnian armies. You see Petkovic, do you remember this name, at the time, at the Bobetko time, one year earlier he was a colonel, now he is General Milivoj Petkovic who was at that time the head of the chief of the HVO. So this is just to show the evolution of the military situation. This agreement, in fact, didn't work. The war between the two parties, the Croats and the Muslims continued, and even the situation worsened in the months to come, May and particularly June, July, August, the war was particularly -- particularly heavy in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, now is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I propose a break. We will have a quarter of an hour's break, please. --- Recess at 12.03 p.m. --- Resumed at 12.20 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you are given the floor, and we will be deliberating until 1.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Professor, just prior to the break, you were going through a series of documents from the international perspective dealing with the question of Croatia's involvement and participation in Bosnia-Herzegovina in '92-'93 and beyond. Can you continue now, please, by referring to those documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next document is document 126 G. This is a document of the United Nations again, it's a document prepared on April 30, 1993, as you can see the date, and with -- this is a report, a report of a delegation which went to visit Bosnia previously. You have here a list of the persons who signed the report. The report is very wide ranging, is taking into consideration different situations, particularly Srebrenica, Gorazde, Zepa where you know the Serb army was particularly involved surrounding the Muslims. It was the period when Morillon went to Srebrenica to save injured people. What is interesting from our point of view is the part on Vitez, because Vitez -- this is page -- sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Nine, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 9, yes. Where the mission -- you have the description, the visit of the missions, they went to Ahmici, they had an opportunity to see what was occurring in those areas, but particularly in the -- of course, we have to take into account this was a mission which arrived immediately after the events. The picture was unclear at that moment. However, it's very interesting that at point 35 on this page 9, as you can see, they asked for a full explanation from the Croat Defence Council on what was going on in Vitez and Central Bosnia, and they spoke to Mr. Boban about this topic. What is interesting is the discussion they had with Boban, points 36 and 37. In a way, even point 40, 41 is interesting as a consequence of this too. You can see here Mr. Boban, with whom the mission met at the airport in Split, denied participation of his forces in these acts; in the acts at Ahmici in Central Bosnia, which he said were the acts of radical groups. And it's very interesting, you see here quoted in brackets "(General Wahlgren had informed us that this group even had swastikas on their clothing)." But you know that there are also documents that the uniformed people -- that if they don't have identity cards of HVO, it was better to have no other insignia, but surely not the Croat army, so every other insignia were possible to be -- were likely to be used. I can tell you, it was very interesting also an episode that occurred in order to understand this event.
