The episode occurred at the beginning of the war in Bosnia, in August 1992, because at that time the Croatian HVO, the HVO was not the only military group of the Croats in Bosnia. At the time, there were also the so-called -- the HOS. The HOS was the organisation, the military organisation, related to the Paraga party, the Hrvatska Stranka Prava, which was the Croat party of the right led by Dobrosav Paraga in Croatia in Zagreb. They had this army, and one of the members of this HOS was general -- general of the HOS, a self-appointed general in this case, and Prkacin who was an elected member of the Croatian Sabor in 1995 under the -- not in the 10 percent of the seats of Herceg-Bosna, his was for Herceg-Bosna, but in the list of the party, of the questioned party of the right. This is just again one element, because it confirmed this particular relation that people had with Zagreb, independently from -- on different levels, yes, on different levels. And this HOS were forced on the -- the idea of the HOS and the idea of the Paraga party was that the whole Bosnia was part of Croatia. The historical dream and the historical borders of Croatia were the Drina river. The Drina is the river which defines the borders between Bosnia and Serbia. So this was different from the agreement or the attempted agreements between the Serb and the Croat side to divide Bosnia, and for this reason, for instance, one of the head of the HOS created a -- at the beginning of the war many troubles. Mr. Kraljevic was killed in August 1993, and after all this, his death, HOS were submitted under the pressure of Boban, so under the command of HVO. So in a sense after August-September 1993, there were no regular units officially out of the control of the HVO. The other point is point 37 where Mr. Boban, while expressing his condemnation of these acts, nevertheless stated that one must not look only at the effects but at the causes, and that Croats had been massacred by Muslims. "The Mission," which was very interested in the reaction, "The Mission expressed its deep concern and told him that these developments could seriously tarnish his image and that of the Croats in general, not to mention the repercussions that it could have on the Republic of Croatia." The attempts justify that in a way Boban made in this situation immediately created a reaction, a negative reaction of the Commission, who had more or less the same -- different but the logic was the same, the reaction by President Tudjman. If you read point 41 where it is stated, for instance, the Mission "conveyed ... shock and horror at the killings by Croats of Muslims in central Bosnia and called upon him to help actively in preventing any recurrence of these outrageous incidents and bringing those responsible to immediate justice. President Tudjman agreed that the acts of inhumanity were unpardonable but said that as long as causes existed for provocation, there may be a temptation to resort to such acts of horror which were typical not only of the Bosnian Croats. He promised to use his influence to see that the guilty were punished." You can see there, in a way, the mechanism was, yes, it is to be condemned, these acts, but you have to understand the situation, the reaction, the tensions. It's, in a way, a kind of justification that created concern in the Mission and in a sense can be interesting in order to understand the reaction of the international representatives in this case. Now we can go further, and document 126 H. This is a document of the Security Council, a document dated May 10th, 1993. It's a note by the President of the Security Council, and what is interesting are particularly paragraphs 3 and 4 where you can see that: "The Security Council strongly condemns this major military offensive launched by Bosnian Croat paramilitary units which is totally inconsistent with the signature of the Peace Plan for the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the Bosnian Croat party." We are in May 1993 and they are considering, of course, the Peace Plan, this is Vance-Owen Plan. "The Council demands that the attacks against the areas of Mostar, Jablanica and Dreznica, cease forthwith; that Bosnian Croat paramilitary units withdraw immediately from the area and that all the parties strictly comply with their previous commitments as well as the cease-fire agreed to today between the Government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Bosnian Croat party." And then you can see in point -- in the last paragraph: "The Security Council once again reiterates its demand that UNPROFOR personnel be allowed unimpeded access throughout the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and, in this particular case, demands that the Bosnian Croat paramilitary units ensure the safety and security of UNPROFOR as well as all United Nations personnel in the areas of Mostar, Jablanica and Dreznica. In this connection, the Council expresses its deep concern at the increasing hostile attitude of Bosnian Croat paramilitary units towards UNPROFOR personnel." The area mentioned is mostly Jablanica, that he is considering, the map, this area in Bosnia. And this means that we can, in this case, understand probably the attempt not to have personnel, UNPROFOR personnel in the area was because they referred to the United Nations Secretary-General for -- and so this was just to give you the atmosphere --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I think on the second page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On the second page, you have point, the first point: "The Security Council calls upon the Republic of Croatia, in accordance with the commitments under the Zagreb agreement of 25 April 1993 ..." This was the agreement signed by Izetbegovic and Boban, witnessed by Tudjman. We saw it before. "... to exert all its influence on the Bosnian Croat leadership and paramilitary units with a view to ceasing immediately their attacks particularly in the areas of Mostar, Jablanica and Dreznica. It further calls on the Republic of Croatia to adhere strictly to its obligations under Security Council resolution 752, including putting an end to all forms of interference and respecting the territorial integrity of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." What is interesting is that the international community was calling upon the Republic of Croatia to influence the position because they were the -- Tudjman was the witness to this agreement between Izetbegovic and Boban, so the international community urged him to make pressure in order to stop the attacks in that area, and the document is interesting because it's from May, so this shows when I ended my -- when I referred in the last session, I'm reminded that the document signed at the end of April of 1993, in fact, was not implemented at all. So this is clear evidence what I said before in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And resolution 752 related withdrawing of troops, did it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the next paragraph that immediately follows after that deals with the question of sovereignty, does it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. "The Security Council once again reaffirms the sovereignty, territorial integrity and independence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the inacceptability of the acquisition of territory by force and the practice of 'ethnic cleansing'." So I think that this is a very clear statement and a result of the pressure of the European -- of the international community in this case towards Croatia. We can go further with the document 126 I.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think we've looked at this one previously, so perhaps we can move on to -- unless you have a particular point that you wish to make about. I'm sorry, I think I'm -- I'm sorry, we haven't looked at it. I'm sorry. I was confusing it with another document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document has been signed in Geneva in July 17, and as you can see, it has been signed by Slobodan Milosevic and Franjo Tudjman. It's a statement of the two Presidents of the two republics which deny speculations about the partition of Bosnia. Point 2 is the crucial point because after denying the partition: "The only way to achieve permanent peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina lies in the recognition of the interests of all the three constituent peoples and in the achievement of the agreement on the establishment of three republics within the scope of a confederation." So in the other situation, we spoke about the federation, a union, now a confederation of three republics, so you see again the attempt to -- as a first step to have three republics in a union and then eventually denying -- the speculation for a partition when you have three republics within the scope of a confederation, which is not clear what this mean -- we don't have, in fact, up to now "confederation," the word, we have a federation, United States and Switzerland are federations. So in this case -- in this case it just means that the three republics can manage together the common interest and then it's -- as a matter of fact in future the integration of Bosnia will be threatened by the -- a new partition, we don't know, of course, peaceful or not. In. Any case, because we see the document -- I remind the document of November 12, 1991 of Grude, when Mate Boban and Dario Kordic signed and established the goals, the main goals of the Croats in Bosnia, this was one part of their goals, the request of one part of their goals to be achieved. At the same time, it is a confirmation that some kind of agreement, or attempt at agreement was going on between Croat and Serb sides about Bosnia, albeit this is just an agreement for creation in Bosnia of three unions. The document offer the possibility for the preparing of another peace plan. It was the Owen-Stoltenberg plan which was submitted a few days after this request. And the proposal was to create, instead of ten cantons, three areas with a predominant ethnic group which was, in fact, more or less the proposal of Tudjman and Milosevic, and this proposal was rejected by the Bosnian parliament in October 1993. As a consequence of this rejection, the relations between Croats and Muslims worsened again and a new phase of war started in that period. This was in the fall 1993 when another event, even worsened the complex picture of the war. This was the, may I say, the serial war within the Muslims, with the secession of the group led by Fikret Abdic in the area of Bihac. Just to show you the map again. This here is Bihac. This was the area. And Fikret Abdic was a member of the presidency of Bosnia after the election in 1990. He was very well known person in the Communist establishment. He led a company, agra commerce, in the '80s, into bankruptcy. I think he was for this reason in prison. So a very disputed personality. What is crucial that in this case a conflict arose within the Muslim groups. Fikret Abdic sought to have, first, a good relationship with Tudjman and then the support of the Serbs, and you see this was an area, a Muslim area, led by Fikret Abdic, but where fighting took place between the Bosnian army and the groups of Abdic and areas surrounded by Serbs because the Serbs controlled this area of Banja Luka and they controlled this area of Croatia which was Krajina. It's just to give you the picture of the situation. So we can continue with other documents. The next one is 126 K. Sorry. I made a mistake, sorry. 126 J. 126 J, yes, this one. This is a letter -- this document of the United Nations, it's a letter of 27 July, 1993, and is a letter from the permanent representative of Bosnia in the United Nations, Mr. Muhamed Sacirbey. The letter is sent, it's included -- a letter received from -- received from the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zagreb, Croatia, that the official television channel of Croatian government and other media calling for demonstration of mass -- for demonstration in Zagreb, and he added the document, the following document, on Croatia -- on the Croatian Charge d'affaires, this is the following page, where you can see, in particular, the description of the situation. "In the area of Vitez," which is a town in Central Bosnia, "the largest Bosnian Croat enclave in central Bosnia," and the letter claims that the population is "threatened by the Bosnian Muslim armed force. We have received the report of high military activity by the Bosnian Muslim army in that area where two Bosnian Croat villages, Zabrdje and Jeliko, on the outskirts of Vitez have already been overrun, and the residents have been expelled. Presently, more than 40,000 refugees, mostly Bosnian Croats, are living in deplorable conditions inside Vitez." This was in a letter in -- that was sent by Sacirbey, and this is a letter that followed the situation in -- let me say, all the attacks of the army -- of the Bosnian army in Central Bosnia when the Croats were defeated and they had to come back again from the centre of Bosnia. So this is -- again, the Bosnian authorities have noted existence of ammunition in Vitez. They are showing how concerned they were in this context for the situation of the Croatian population in a period of offensive made by the army of Bosnia. On the other side we have the concern of Mr. Sacirbey about organisation and demonstration in Croatia of what was going on in Zagreb. So this can offer to -- a different picture of two -- of situation of tensions that was not only in Bosnia but created tensions between Bosnia and Zagreb too. We can go further, on document 126 K.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that was a letter attached to that, it's the second paragraph of the letter that you ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the second paragraph of the -- is an information that claimed in November, more or less when the offensive of the army was going on -- Bosnian army was going on in Central Bosnia, the old bridge in Mostar was destroyed by the Croatian army. "On this day ... the Croatian army and the Croatian Defence Council has destroyed the most significant monument of Bosnian-Herzogovinian culture." This is a document -- official protest from the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina informing the Security Council what was happening and they charged the Croatian army was taking part in the military operation in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And is this more or less a continuation of the issues -- of the cooperation between the Croatian army and the Defence Council that you referred to when you looked at the Bogatca documents of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next one is 126 -- sorry, 126 L.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, it's another letter, and if you would look at the third paragraph of the letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The third paragraph of the letter is -- this letter is a letter of -- signed by Izetbegovic, it was signed in November of 1993, to the Secretary-General, and he's stressing that -- this is very important. This was the position of the Bosnian government, the official position of the Bosnian government, when you can see it's written that "the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina is not a conflict of" -- this is the protest -- "of three sides, as stated in your letter. It is an open and brutal aggression against an independent State, which is a Member State of the United Nations. A direct consequence of the aggression has been the establishment of phantom para-states in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." Phantom para-states are to be considered Herceg-Bosna from one side and the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the other side. "... which was followed by a legitimacy given by the international community, taking them as the sides to the conflict. It is not possible to conduct a peace process successfully having such hypotheses on its grounds."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is meant by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What do you understand him to be saying there? What's the purpose that he's trying to convey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the question is that, in fact, the two para-states are acting for other two neighbour states and they are connected with them, so in this case the claim is that they were involved in order to divide Bosnia and not as a conflict within Bosnia and a conflict -- civil conflict, a civil conflict in a state but an aggression coming from Serbia and Croatia and, in this case, an international conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the next document, 126 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next document is 126 M.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I think -- the annex again is the interesting part of that, is it not, in the first paragraph -- first and second paragraphs of the annex.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This a document -- this is a letter sent on 28 January, 1994, so we are in a new year, 1994. It was sent by the Prime Minister of Bosnia, Haris Silajdzic, and was sent to the President of Security Council, and the letter is -- includes in the centre -- here in the -- after the second paragraph, it includes a list from the -- information of the government, a list of the military actions carried in the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina by brigades of the Croat army. So you can see the description of the brigade of Split, the brigade from Zagreb, the brigade from Srebrenica, Osijek, Vukovar, Vinkovci, Varazdin, and you have a list of different units of the army, and this was the list submitted by the Bosnian government to the United Nations to show who was participating in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And this letter is dated the 28th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And over the page, I think there's a reference, is there not, in the centre of the page, the paragraph: "Thus we conclude." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The final paragraph of the -- you mean the final paragraph of the letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I don't mean that. I meant the paragraph which is the fourth paragraph on the second -- on page 3, which is the last page of the letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, yes, on the Posavina front in the Sector of Orasje, four brigades of the Croatian army. I can't see in the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You've got the wrong page. It's the next page I want you to refer to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you refer to the next page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second page?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. It becomes the third page. You see the paragraph "Thus we conclude."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "We express our deep concern."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, the top.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the top?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: "Thus we conclude." The paragraph starting "Thus we conclude." It's the fourth paragraph down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, "Thus we conclude," yes, yes, "we 0082 conclude that in the sector of Mostar, Prozor and Gornji Vakuf, twelve brigades of the regular Croatian army with manpower estimated at 15,000 to 18,000 soldiers is directly involved in military operations." You see, this 15,000 is the number which was estimated by the International Institute for Strategic Studies when we saw yesterday the figures about the forces arrayed in Bosnia, and this was more or less the evolution in 1993, beginning 1994. "... involved in military operations. In the Posavina sector," which is the north of Bosnia, "the estimate goes as far as 10,000 to 12,000 soldiers of the Croatian army. Accordingly, the estimate ranges from 25,000 to 30,000 soldiers of the Croatian army actively participating in military operations against the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." This was the conclusion from the Bosnian point of view, from the Bosnian official, from the Bosnian government point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And the next paragraph I think --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "This high number of Croatian regular army troops are supplemented by heavy artillery, armoured vehicles and numerous other war materials" coming from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And again is this a development and progression of what was happening in 1992 when General --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's a progression we can see in the other documents prepared directly by -- in the following documents prepared by the United Nations, their estimation, thanks to the possibility of UNPROFOR personnel to check the information. So this was the position of the government. But the following document, for instance, the 126 N, is a document of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, this one's dated 2nd February, 1994, I think?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the 2nd February, yes. The previous document was the 28th of January. So four days after. And this is a document -- this is signed by the -- Secretary-General of the United Nations, Mr. Boutros Boutros-Ghali, and was -- is a letter addressed by him, the 2nd February -- the 1st February, from the Secretary-General to the President of the Security Council. And what is interesting is particularly the third paragraph: "The Croatian Army has directly supported the HVO in terms of manpower, equipment and weapons for some time. Initially the level of support was limited to individual and small sub-units, many of them volunteers. As the offensives of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Government forces against the HVO have become successful, the numbers of Croatian soldiers appear to have increased. It is assessed that in total there is the equivalent of three Croatian Brigades of regular Army personnel in Bosnia and Herzegovina, approximately 3,000 to 5,000 (this is an estimation ...)" This is important. "(... as it is impossible with UNPROFOR's assets to obtain required information for a more accurate account). There have been confirmed reports by UNPROFOR personnel that elements (troops and equipment) from the following Croatian Army (HV) units are indeed present in central and southern Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then you see the list of the personnel, the elements, on the basis of the UNPROFOR personnel, which kind of brigade were operating in the central and southern Bosnia and Herzegovina from the Croatian army. Then you have the list of the army. Then you have the following paragraph in the following page explaining that: "Equipment includes heavy artillery and multi-barrelled rocket launchers," so "Most recently" and "is unable to confirm positively any Croatian Army tank activity in Bosnia and Herzegovina." So there was no clear evidence of this; they didn't have. "Also in January ... confirmed that four helicopter flights from Croatia crossed into Bosnia and Herzegovina." They have different information but information that, however, a certain number of brigades and soldiers of the Croatian army were acting in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the period between 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, just going back, I think, to document 123 that we haven't looked at, exhibit 123, it's a -- it was one of the documents that I think was ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You may not be able to get it -- see if you can find it there. It's 123, exhibit 123. It's a Security Council document of the 3rd of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. This is the 3rd of February, the day after.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of this letter sent by Mr. Boutros Boutros-Ghali. This is the number 123.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think it's the first paragraph that's particularly interesting, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first paragraph: "The Security Council is deeply concerned that the Republic of Croatia has deployed elements of the Croatian Army along with heavy military equipment in the central and southern parts of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as described in the Secretary-General's letter of 1 February 1994," the letter we read before. And then you can see the fourth paragraph is: "The Security Council demands that the Republic of Croatia withdraw forthwith all elements of the Croatian Army (HV)" -- you see there the symbol -- "along with military equipment and fully respect the territorial integrity of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." What is interesting even more is the first paragraph of the next page of this document: "The Security Council will consider other serious measures if the Republic of Croatia fails to put an immediate end to all forms of interference in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." This is a very important topic because this is a first official threat to Zagreb with sanctions. As far as I know, the first policy maker who spoke about sanctions and threatened Croatia with sanctions was the German Minister of Foreign Affairs, Klaus Kinkel, in May 1993 when he was in Zagreb, and he spoke to Tudjman and he was very concerned about the policy of Croatian government. The international community also in November put pressures on Tudjman because they considered that a particular responsibility of the Croatian army was -- in November where it destroyed the villages of Pocitelj and Divoselo, and Tudjman promised to hold an inquiry in this sense. Then we had other threats of sanctions particularly in February, this is February 1994, when Kohl made a dramatic speech on the television in February 1994 and even the Italian Minister of Foreign Affairs, Andreatta, threatened Zagreb with sanctions in that month. So this was the month for putting the firm international pressure on the Croatian government in order to obtain the withdrawal of the Croatian army units in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now can we go on to the next document, 126 N, which is again a document of the 2nd of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And it's a letter, is it not, from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: -- from Croatia, the permanent representative for Croatia, United Nations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a letter -- yes. A letter of February 2nd, 1994. It was written by the permanent representative of Croatia in -- at the United Nations, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The second paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second paragraph is very crucial: "My government," it is written, "does not deny that there are regular Croatian Army troops in the border areas between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They are stationed there in accordance with the Joint Agreement of 12 July 1992" -- probably this was a mistake, typewritten mistake, the agreement was of the 21st of July -- anyway -- "between my Government and the Government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Repositioning of these troops would seriously undermine the territorial integrity and security of the Republic of Croatia." This -- the agreement between -- which is mentioned here in this letter was signed on July 21st, 1992 by Izetbegovic and Tudjman, and it considered that HVO was a part of the army, of the Bosnian army, and, secondly, it was written that cooperation between the Croatian army and the Bosnian army was possible along the borders, but any future military alliance between the two countries will be taken into consideration only, only in the event that the international community has failed in attempts at stopping the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina." So it was under the condition. And immediately after the signing of this document, Tudjman put pressure again on Izetbegovic in order to have a more complete alliance and federation or confederation but Izetbegovic rejected the proposal all the time. So this was the agreement and this important -- interesting -- it is interesting --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just before you move on, I think the fact of the matter is, is it not, the HVO did not at any stage come under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, no. In fact, HVO acted as an independent army in the sense that you see there were attempts in July, attempts -- the agreement was that it was -- it had to be part of the army. Later, in April, in April 1993, it was signed again, the document we see, between Mate Boban and Izetbegovic, is annexed to the other one with the witness of Tudjman. It was stated that HVO will have a representative in the army, but these agreements didn't work. The attempt was not -- on the contrary, in the beginning -- at the beginning of 1993, we have the order of Prlic, the head of HVO, the President, which established that in the cantons of the provisional plan assigned to Croatia, the commander of the army had to be submitted to the HVO command. So you have, in this case, the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you cite this nevertheless in support for your proposition that the HVO and the army of Croatia, the HV, had a sort of continuity in Bosnia-Herzegovina right from '92 through to '95.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I can say, my personal opinion was that this was the same army, same army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The connection were so strong that we can -- from the political point of view, the approach from the political -- as a political scientist, I can say that the main impression was that this was the same army. I would like just to turn your attention even to the sentence on the second page of the letter of Nobilo, Mario Nobilo. This is: "Under such circumstances, where the Council doesn't have the resources to protect the Croat citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, my Government has no moral right to prevent the Croatian volunteers from helping the imperilled Bosnian Croat community, which makes up 18 percent of the country's population, but has been expelled onto 10 percent of the country's territory." So this sentence is important in order to consider the following letter. This was the official statement generally defended by the Croatian government, that people fighting in Bosnia was citizens of Bosnia, were born in Bosnia, were volunteers without any control, official control from the Croatian army. This was the official position of the Croatian government at that point. But if you look at the following document, number 126 P, this document is a document -- is a letter again sent on 16 February, 1994, through the permanent representative Mario Nobilo, the Croatian permanent representative in the United Nations sent by Mate Granic, the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Foreign Affairs of Croatia to the Secretary-General. This letter, I would like to turn your attention in particular to page 3, the fourth and the fifth paragraphs, where we are informed that: "As a peace-promoting step in cooperation with the Security Council and as a goodwill gesture towards the Sarajevo Government, in the meantime my Government expresses its readiness to withdraw certain units from the border areas with Bosnia and Herzegovina, in accordance with the recent Security Council request." This again is consistent with the letter, the previous letter, sent by Mr. Nobilo. "But my government," Croatian government, of course, "calls upon the Government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina immediately to order its army to cease all hostilities and offensive actions against Croatian population centres, especially in the region of central Bosnia. Following the cessation of hostilities, we shall issue an appeal to all Croat volunteers in central Bosnia to lay down their arms and return to their normal civilian lives." So this is another element. And then it is interesting, the following sentence: "The Republic of Croatia is ready to call off the units of the Croatian Army on the left bank of the Neretva River and elements of the Croatian Army on the right bank on the Neretva." I would like to show you just a moment a map of Bosnia, if I can say again, just to give you a picture. This is again map 114, because it's clear. And you can see Bosnia and where the Neretva River is. So the left bank is this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO NAVIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, I cannot change my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Nor can I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me. Do we have a technical problem since my colleague judges cannot follow on the screen, on the monitor, the document. I personally can. I have the images. I would kindly ask the technical service to inform me -- yes, on one of the screens, we do have the image of the map. On the other one, we do not. Obviously, we do have a problem. Now everything is all right. I think everything is under control now. Do we all have the images on the screen? I think there are some disturbances in the transmission because when I have an image on, picture on the screen -- excuse me -- we could continue if we get the picture back. But in the meantime, it has changed again. We're speaking of document 124. Continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Now I lost my picture on the monitor, but doesn't matter. You can see here on the map the Neretva River, which the document speaks about, Mate Granic is speaking about the units of the Croatian army on the left bank, which is this one, and volunteers, volunteers -- and the elements. One is the -- one of the elements of the Croatian army. The units of the Croatian army are on the left bank, this here, and the elements of the Croatian army on the right bank. So you can see that it's difficult to say that they were exactly along the border, albeit that they were not only in a point near to the border, you know? So this is, in a way, a kind of admission from the Deputy Prime Minister that the army was -- the Croatian army was in the territory of Herzegovina along the river Neretva instead of the borders. A kind of confirmation is in the following documents. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Because I think if you go to exhibit 126 Q, and in particular the fourth paragraph starting on the 10th February, "UNPROFOR observed." Fourth paragraph, first page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fourth paragraph, yes. Fourth paragraph. Yes. "On 10 February, UNPROFOR observed a convoy ..." This letter is the letter of 17 February, and it comes from Secretary-General Boutros-Ghali to the President of the Security Council, so it's information coming from the personnel of the UNPROFOR to the Secretary-General, and then the Secretary-General is referring to the President of the Security Council in February. And in this letter it is written that UNPROFOR -- in the fourth paragraph it is written that "UNPROFOR observed a convoy of the Croatian Defence Council (HVO), consisting of 21 trucks and other equipment, leaving the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina via the Lipa checkpoint," which is a little bit strange that a convoy of HVO, that is, of the Croatian army -- the Bosnian Croatia army was going to Croatia in this period. "One of these trucks had markings of the Fifth HV Brigade." That is the Fifth Croatian Army Brigade. "The convoy also included a bus carrying 36 soldiers with insignia of an independent Croatian Army unit from Zagreb. The event was videotaped by a uniformed cameraman of the (Croatian army) or (the Croatian Army of Bosnia.)" So in this case, it is informing that something is going on, some withdrawal is going on, and UNPROFOR officials were noticing that troops with different insignia were crossing the borders toward Croatia. The same document, in the following page, page 2, you can see in the third paragraph: "In the absence of any observations of (a Croatian Army) withdrawal movements beyond that on 10 February, UNPROFOR continues to assess that there still may be 5,000 (Croatian Army) troops in Bosnia and Herzegovina, although no (Croatian Army) command posts nor any full (Croatian Army) brigades operating as formed units have been identified." So they estimate because the problem was that they didn't have insignia. And in this sense -- it appears -- the following sentence is also interesting: "It appears that (Croatian Army) troops are now being more circumspect ..." This is interesting. "... and may be removing their (Croatian Army) insignia while in Bosnia and Herzegovina and replacing them with those of the HVO. UNPROFOR believes that (Croatian Army) insignia on a number of vehicles has been erased or repainted." Which is consistent with orders received since 1992 from Bobetko. We can go further. Another document is 126 R. This is a letter of 17 February, 1994, the same date -- the same day of the previous document. The letter was sent by the Ambassador Nobilo as the Croatian representative to the United Nations, to the Secretary-General, and these two paragraphs, the second and the third, are interesting enough. The first one informs us that "Croatian volunteers that had been situated" -- we are speaking about volunteers -- "that had been situated in the Uskoplje-Rama area in Central Bosnia" -- so this is Central Bosnia -- "have returned to the Republic of Croatia on 10 February 1994. The convoy consisted of 24 [sic] vehicles with 12 heavy artillery weapons, 3 buses, and 650 volunteers --"

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think that's 44 vehicles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It says here 44 vehicles, yeah. The second paragraph informs us that on 16 February, six days after, at 10.00 hours "elements of the Croatian Army" -- not anymore volunteers, "elements of the Croatian Army left the wider Neretva river region." You say "wider" means something very generic but wide, more than wide. So if you look again at the map 114 and you see the river Neretva area and you can see in this case the term "wider Neretva river region," this means it is not just some point but wider means an area large enough to include all the regions existing around the Neretva river. So this means -- this is another admission that elements -- at least elements of the Croatian Army were in wider Neretva region until 16 February, 1994. And the document goes on: "... and I have been repositioned in the Metkovic area," Metkovic is in Croatia, "on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. I have received information from my authorities that amongst the aforesaid elements of the Croatian Army were 600 soldiers, 4 battle tanks and 6 heavy artillery pieces." So they had to admit that anyway. They have tanks, artillery pieces, and soldiers in the wider Neretva River region.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think, Professor, it is now half past one, and Your Honours may wish to adjourn at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: We will adjourn our hearing. I believe that only two documents still remain to be discussed; is it not so? Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's some other documents, but I'll be very short in the morning. I wouldn't expect to be longer than an hour at most, but I'm just about ready to wrap up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Okay. We will therefore adjourn the hearing for today, and tomorrow we will reconvene at 9.00 a.m. Thank you, Professor.
